Did you remember to add the “count” attribute. You need more than 2 bytes to represent a double long unsign.

removing the safety lines does not make modbus read more bytes, and thus theresult you get are not correct.

@nikito7 please add the configuration for that sensor. I think you might miss “count: 2” which are needed to read 4 bytes, uint32 is 2 registers, uint16 is 1 register. A register is pr modbus standard 16bit.

Just to follow up, we are constantly testing a.o. the following configurations.

```
            {
```

- UINT seems to work
- SCALE with or with out PRECISION seems to work

So in case something does not work, please submit:
- the configuration of the failing sensor.
- the modbus RECEIVE lines (hex bytes)
- the wrong result
- the wanted result

You need to be careful and secure the count is big enough the read the number of bytes used by the configured datatype/struct.

with out sanity check work perfect

It's only 1 register

There are two types:
- 2 registers: 0x1234 and 0x5678 
- 1 register only: 0x12345678

```
> 01 04 00 26 00 01 d0 01 
: 01 04 04 00 1a b1 1c af da
```

001ab11c = 1749276 it's the correct response

“ 1 register only: 0x12345678” this do not exist in the modbus standard. 1 Register is 16 bit = 2 bytes, so it might be stated in the manual as 1 register but at protocol level it is 2 registers.

So count = 2, reads 2 registers = 4 bytes.

“ 001ab11c = 1749276 it's the correct response” that assumes count=2 because you read 4 bytes.

you dont need to believe me see this link:
https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modbus

inout/holding registers are 16bit...not 32!   but a manual is written from a user perspective and often says 1 value is stored in 1 register....and most times is says in “2 words” == 2 modbus registers.

Well to answer both of you....which modbus command reads 4 bytes with count = 1 ? You are mixing issue, I talk about the modbus protocol. We cannot do things not defined in the modbus protocol. 

I know a devices have values like float, int32 or even bigger ones, but at the protocol layer those are read as multiple modbus protocol registers.

If you look above you see long is 2 bytes and double long is 4 bytes....then please compare that to the modbus protocol and you will see:

Reading a long from a holding register function code ox03 is done with count=1
Reading a double long from a holding register function code ox03 is done with count=2
because a holding register is according to the modbus definition 2 bytes.

The pdf I just got also in chapter 5 specifies how many bytes are needed to store each data type. and in 5.4.1.1 it explains how function code 0x04 (semi identical to 0x03) works, remark the "Quantity of of input registers" which is exactly what "count: x" refers to. I like the comment "short answer: DATA_TYPE_UINT32", problem is only that it does not exist at protocol level.

But I think we should stop the discussion here, you all seem to know how the modbus protocol works a lot better than me (for reference I am an engineer who have and are implementing modbus protocols in devices and servers for 20+ years), so feel free to submit a patch to the modbus integration.
